name: Pulo Annian, the Pulo Anna dialect of Sonsorol
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.
catalog_citation: Rehg, Kenneth L. 1993. Proto-Micronesian prosody. In Jerold A. Edmondson & Kenneth J. Gregerson (eds.), Tonality in Austronesian Languages (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 24), 25-46. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press, p. 32 (a hypothesis built on the Pulo Annian intonation data of Oda, Sachiko. 1977. The Syntax of Pulo Annian: A Nuclear Micronesian Language. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa), as relayed by Vita, Vasiliki. 2020. Prosodic Patterns in Ramari Hatohobei. MA dissertation (Language Documentation and Description), SOAS University of London, 81 pp., p. 19 and fn. 1.
catalog_locator: Vita 2020, p. 19, section 4 'Micronesian Prosody', paragraph beginning 'In those languages with an incomplete vowel-weakening process', plus footnote 1 on the same page; file, re- with. Rehg 1993: 32 itself not opened.
catalog_quote: Oda (1977, in Regh, 1993: 32) notes that the intonation contour of a simple statement in Pulo Annian, a question-word question and a simple command is 231, with no pitch levels presented, and Regh (1993: 32) inferring that pitch level 3 is assigned on the penultimate mora. These conclusions are noted as hypothetical and if forms like the ones above occur in Pulo Annian, then, stress assignment is mora-sensitive while pitch assignment is syllable-structure sensitive (Regh, 1993: 32). That way, stress is assigned on the penultimate voiced mora, with voiceless moras being treated as extrametrical, and high pitch assigned to the penultimate syllable. Thus, stress and pitch might not co occur because of final vowel devoicing. [fn. 1] Oda’s (1977) dissertation on Pulo Annian (Glottocode pulo1240) was not possible to retrieve and the data presented here is from Regh’s (1993) paper on Proto-Micronesian prosody (Figure 4).
sweep_summary: Sonsorol (sons1242) is not in the catalog; the world-target record named Capell 1969 as its source and marked it unreachable. The one stress-title item, Vita (2020) 'Prosodic Patterns in Ramari Hatohobei' (SOAS MA thesis, 81 pp.), was located and downloaded in full via CORE (mirror of SOAS Research Online, whose old eprints host no longer resolves) and read: section 6.2.1 (p. 37) states that Tobian is weight-sensitive with primary stress (intensity) on the penultimate mora of the prosodic word, with refinements for disyllables with sonorant codas (pp. 38-41); pitch is syllable-structure sensitive and does not coincide with stress; secondary stress not investigated. The thesis also reports (p. 16) that Capell 1969 and van den Berg 2014 contain no prosody information, which lowers the priority of acquiring Capell. A second open paper by the same author on Sonsorolese proper (Vita & Pedro 2021, SOAS WPL 20) was also downloaded and is silent on stress placement. Wikipedia's Tobian page lists penult/final/antepenult stress without a usable source. Everything with. Best new statement: Vita 2020: 37 (penultimate-mora, weight-sensitive), applicable to the Tobian variety; no catalog source exists to supersede.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Hypothesis (Rehg's, relayed by Vita): primary stress falls on the penultimate voiced mora of the word, counting from the right; word-final devoiced/voiceless vowels do not count (extrametrical), so a word with a devoiced final vowel is stressed on the last voiced mora minus one; high pitch (level 3 of a 231 contour) sits on the penultimate syllable. Mora-counting with long vowels/diphthongs bimoraic makes this weight-sensitive rather than syllable-penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Pulo Annian/Sonsorol. (For Tobian, Vita 2020: 37 and 68 hypothesizes secondary stress on the mora preceding the primary, alternating leftward, as in other Micronesian languages.)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the whole rule is explicitly labelled hypothetical, inferred from sentence intonation contours rather than from measured word stress. Vita 2020: 17 also states that Capell 1969 and van den Berg 2014 contain no information on prosody.
new_statements.domain_note: Derived from phrase-level intonation contours (statements, WH-questions, commands all 231) in Oda 1977, projected onto word/mora level by Rehg 1993; concerns the Pulo Anna dialect (Glottolog pulo1240) of Sonsorol, not Sonsorol island speech (Ramari Dongosaro).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog attaches Vita 2020 to sons1242, but that thesis's first-hand instrumental statement (p. 37: primary stress on the penultimate mora of the prosodic word) describes Ramari Hatohobei = Tobian, ISO tox, Glottolog tobi1238, a sister language that is a separate target in our catalog; it should be credited there, not to Sonsorol. The only Sonsorol-specific statement found is the second-hand Rehg 1993 hypothesis about the Pulo Anna dialect (Glottolog pulo1240, dialect of sons1242), relayed by Vita 2020: 19. Sonsorol island speech (Ramari Dongosaro) has no located stress statement; Vita & Pedro 2021 describe it without one.

new_statements.quote: Tobian is weight-sensitive and seems to be following the hypothesis about the Pulo Annian pattern (Regh, 1993: 32), with stress assignment (intensity) being mora sensitive. Primary stress is assigned on the penultimate (from left to right) mora of the prosodic word. For example, in fioŋo-ri, story-of (Figure 19 and Table 7), a quadrimoraic prosodic word, fi/o/ŋo/ri, it is the penultimate mora ŋ[o]=73.32 dB that presents the highest intensity, while secondary stress is assigned on the preceding mora, fi[o]=72.82 dB.
new_statements.citation: Vita, Vasiliki (2020). Prosodic Patterns in Ramari Hatohobei. MA dissertation, SOAS, University of London. 81 pp.
new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive, mora-counting stress: primary stress on the penultimate mora of the prosodic word (instrumental: intensity peak), with heavy syllables (diphthongs, long vowels, sonorant codas, probably geminate m:) counting two moras; in disyllables with a heavy penult the second mora of that syllable is stressed. Pitch peak does not coincide with stress. Secondary stress hypothesized on preceding moras but not studied. This is the Tobian (Ramari Hatohobei) variety of the Sonsorol-Tobi group, from an MA thesis based on archival recordings; the author says the only grammar (Capell 1969) and the other sketch (van den Berg 2014) contain no prosody information, so this is the first stress statement for the group. For a catalog's classification of sons1242 it supports a 'penultimate mora / weight-sensitive right-edge' classification, with the caveat that Sonsorolese proper (Ramari Dongosaro) has no first-hand stress statement yet.

new_statements.quote: Sonsorol has both stress and pitch accent or tone. [...] tone does not serve to distinguish meaning in this language, i.e., it is not a tonal language [...] The stress accent is marked, but not excessively so [...] While there can be little doubt that the accent normally fell on the last syllable but one in the older form of the language, at the present day it may also fall on the final syllable or the last but two. [...] The bulk of simple Sonsorol words of two syllables carry the accent on the last but one. [...] The addition of such a suffix may cause the stress to change. [...] The basic rule of the language is still that the stress falls on the last syllable but one of a word.

new_statements.relation_note: TYPE differs. The catalog record (weight-hedged, via Vita 2020: 19 relaying Rehg 1993: 32 on Oda's 1977 Pulo Annian data) is a hypothetical mora-counting analysis: stress on the penultimate (voiced) mora. Capell 1969 (first-hand, 1947-48 CIMA fieldwork, describing 'Sonsorol' with Pul = Pulo Anna and Merir said to agree closely with Sonsorol, Tobi more divergent) states a syllable-counting default: 'the basic rule.. stress falls on the last syllable but one of a word', with lexically listed final-stress and antepenult-stress words and one stress minimal pair, i.e. penultimate with lexical exceptions rather than weight-sensitive. PLACEMENT largely coincides: CV.CV words are penult under both;…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (a 'stress accent', moderate in strength) falls as the basic rule on the penultimate syllable of the word; a class of words has final stress (me'ta 'what?', ri'weis 'child', ta'mor 'chief'; word-final diphthongs are stressed on their first element, i'tei 'my name', fi'touw 'how many?'), which Capell attributes historically to loss of a final syllable or to an added transitive -i, and a 'fairly numerous' but lexically limited class of common words has antepenultimate stress ('jalimat 'person', 'kamara 'his actions') that 'must be learned by hearing'. Grammatical suffixes may shift the stress; stress can occasionally distinguish words (faruje 'to draw, tattoo' vs fa'ruje 'island, village'). Pitch/tone variation is rich but non-contrastive ('it is not a tonal language'). In sense-groups a major accent is often thrown back onto the verbal particle, and enclitics (e.g. -me, i:a 'where?') pull the accent of the preceding word one syllable rightward.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary word stress; section 4 'Sentence Stress' describes phrase-level accent shifts (accent thrown back to the verbal particle e; enclitics advancing the preceding word's accent by a syllable) and suggests sentence stress links with the pitch pattern of phrases.
new_statements.exceptions: final-stressed words (historically lost final syllable; transitive -i forms such as do'pi, yatoa'di:); final diphthongs stressed on first element; antepenult-stressed common words to be learned individually; suffixation may move stress; one minimal pair by stress (faruje / fa'ruje); enclitic-induced shift.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell describes 'the language of Sonsorol-Tobi' from 1947-48 CIMA fieldwork, taking Sonsorol (Dono'sa:ru) as the base and treating Pul (Pulo Ana, Pu:r), Merir and Tobi as dialects; he says Pul and Merir 'usually agree more closely with Sonsorol' and Tobi has 'more marked peculiarities of pronunciation'. The accent section is stated for Sonsorol generally, not specifically for the Pulo Anna dialect named in the item; the catalog record's source (Rehg 1993 on Oda 1977) is specifically Pulo Annian.

readall_conflicts: Capell 1969 (first-hand, Part I pp. 10-12) gives a syllable-based rule, penultimate stress as 'the basic rule of the language' with lexically listed final-stressed and antepenult-stressed words, a stress minimal pair (faruje/fa'ruje), stress shifts under suffixation and enclisis, and non-contrastive tone; the catalog's only record is Rehg's 1993 hypothesis (relayed by Vita 2020: 19) that Pulo Annian stress is mora-sensitive (penultimate mora), classified weight-hedged/weight-sensitive. The two agree on placement for most words (penult in CV.CV words; Capell's final diphthongs stressed on the first element = penultimate mora; his final-stress-after-lost-syllable words match Rehg's extrametrical voiceless final mora), but differ in type: Capell's account is fixed penult with lexical exceptions (including an antepenult class the mora rule does not generate), not quantity-driven. Capell also refutes the note held by the project (from Vita 2020: 17) that his grammar has no prosody information. Vita 2020: 37's first-hand penultimate-mora finding is for Tobian (tobi1238), which Capell singles out as the most divergent dialect.
